subject: phy
title: Deformation of Solids
subtitle: Hooke's law, elastic/plastic behaviour, stress, strain and Young modulus.
concept: Hooke's law: extension is proportional to force, up to the limit of proportionality; beyond the elastic limit, permanent deformation occurs.
Stress (σ = F/A) and strain (ε = e/L₀) are intensive quantities; the Young modulus E = σ/ε is a material property.
The area under a force–extension graph gives the elastic energy (strain energy) stored.

notes.heading: Hooke's Law and the Force–Extension Graph
items: Hooke's law: for a spring or wire below the limit of proportionality, the extension e is proportional to the applied force F: F = ke, where k is the spring constant (N m⁻¹). The gradient of a linear F–e graph = k.

The limit of proportionality is the point beyond which F ∝ e no longer holds. The elastic limit is (close to but) beyond the limit of proportionality — if exceeded, the material undergoes permanent deformation and does not return to its original length when the load is removed.

notes.heading: Stress, Strain and Young Modulus
items: Tensile stress σ = F/A (Pa = N m⁻²) — the force per unit cross-sectional area. Tensile strain ε = e/L₀ — the fractional extension (dimensionless, no units).
Young modulus E = σ/ε = (F/A)/(e/L₀). Units: Pa. E is a material property — it describes intrinsic stiffness, independent of the sample's dimensions. The gradient of a linear stress–strain graph = E.
Spring constant k is not a material property — it depends on both material (E) and dimensions: k = EA/L₀.

notes.heading: Elastic Strain Energy
items: Energy stored in a stretched spring or wire (within Hooke's law): E_el = ½Fe = ½ke². This equals the area under the F–e graph (a triangle for a Hookean material).
Elastic deformation: energy stored is fully recovered when the load is removed. Plastic deformation: energy is dissipated as heat; the loading and unloading curves differ (hysteresis loop).

notes.heading: Material Properties from Stress–Strain Graphs
items: Ductile materials (e.g. mild steel, copper) show a large plastic region — they can be drawn into wire. The yield point marks the onset of large plastic strain with little additional stress.
Brittle materials (e.g. glass, cast iron) fracture with little or no plastic deformation — the stress–strain graph is linear almost to the breaking point.
The ultimate tensile stress (UTS) is the maximum stress a material can withstand before necking and fracture.

definitions.body: The extension of a spring (or wire) is proportional to the applied force, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded: F = ke.
The ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain: E = σ/ε; units Pa; a material property independent of size and shape.
The maximum force (or stress) beyond which a material undergoes permanent deformation and will not return to its original dimensions.
The energy stored in a deformed elastic material: E_el = ½Fe = ½ke²; equals the area under the F–e graph.

workedExamples.q: A steel wire of length 2.00 m and cross-sectional area 1.00 × 10⁻⁶ m² extends by 1.60 mm when a 100 N load is applied. Calculate the Young modulus.

mistakes: Confusing the limit of proportionality (F ∝ e ends) with the elastic limit (permanent deformation begins) — they are close but not identical.
Using k (spring constant) when the question asks for E (Young modulus) — they are different quantities.
Forgetting the factor of ½ in strain energy: E_el = ½Fe, not Fe.
tips: Young modulus calculation: write F, A, e, L₀ clearly, then calculate σ and ε before dividing.
Area under F–e graph = strain energy; for a triangle (Hooke's law region): area = ½ × base × height = ½Fe.
Material vs shape: E is a material property; k depends on length and area (k = EA/L₀).

flashcards.a: F = ke; extension is proportional to force, up to the limit of proportionality.
E = σ/ε = (F/A)/(e/L₀); units Pa; a material property relating stress to strain.

flashcards.q: What is the strain energy stored in a spring at extension e?
flashcards.a: E_el = ½ke² = ½Fe (area under the F–e graph).

flashcards.q: What is the difference between elastic and plastic deformation?
flashcards.a: Elastic: material returns to original shape when force removed. Plastic: permanent deformation remains.
Stress σ = F/A (Pa); strain ε = e/L₀ (dimensionless).

flashcards.q: A material has a large plastic region on its stress–strain graph. What type of material is it?
flashcards.a: Ductile (e.g. copper, mild steel) — can be drawn into wires or shaped without fracturing.

questions.q: A spring with k = 400 N m⁻¹ extends by 0.05 m. What is the elastic energy stored?
What does the gradient of a stress–strain graph give (in the linear region)?
questions.exp: Gradient = σ/ε = Young modulus (in the linear/proportional region).

questions.q: Stress has the SI unit of:
A material fractures without significant plastic deformation. What type is it?
questions.exp: Brittle materials (e.g. glass, cast iron) fracture suddenly with little plastic deformation.

questions.q: A wire of length L₀ and area A has Young modulus E. What is its spring constant k?
questions.exp: From F = ke and E = FL₀/(Ae): k = F/e = EA/L₀.

recall: State Hooke's law and identify the spring constant from a F–e graph.
Define stress, strain and Young modulus and state their units.
Calculate the Young modulus from experimental data.
Calculate strain energy from the area under a F–e graph.
Distinguish between elastic, plastic, ductile and brittle behaviour.

summary.label: Hooke's law
summary.value: F = ke (up to limit of proportionality)

summary.label: Ductile vs brittle
summary.value: ductile: large plastic region; brittle: fractures early
